answer: An important lesson I have learned in life is that failure is not something to be feared, but a valuable teacher. I learned this the hard way, after failing at something I had worked hard for and initially feeling completely [[demoralised]]. After school, I prepared for months for the admission test of a well-known public university, but I missed out on a place by a small margin. For weeks, I barely wanted to leave the house, and I felt I had let my parents down. In time, however, I came to see that the setback taught me far more than easy success ever could. I went on to study business administration at another university, worked hard and discovered a field I truly enjoy. This lesson is important because the fear of failure holds so many people back from even trying. Once I embraced the idea that mistakes are simply part of growth, I became far more [[resilient]] and willing to take risks. Honestly, this shift in mindset has been genuinely [[transformative]]. I now approach challenges with curiosity rather than dread. It has affected every area of my life, from my career to my personal relationships. At work, I now share this story with students who receive rejection letters, and it seems to [[reassure]] them. I think it is one of the most [[liberating]] realisations a person can have. Understanding that failing is part of succeeding has given me the courage to pursue things I once would have avoided entirely, including my plan to study abroad.

followUps.q: How did your parents react when you failed that test?
followUps.answer: Much better than I expected. My father told me he had faced many losses in business and still recovered, and my mother simply cooked my favourite food. Their calm reaction really helped me move on.

followUps.q: Do you think schools should teach this lesson?
followUps.answer: Yes, definitely. Schools here focus so heavily on results that children see failure as shameful. Teachers could [[normalise]] mistakes by showing how every expert once struggled as a beginner.

note: Made the failure concrete (missing a public university place by a small margin), added how he recovered via his BBA, and sharing the story with students at work; added [[reassure]].
